# Migrate from Stable Foldkit

This guide starts with an application on the current stable Foldkit APIs and ends with the APIs documented by this integration preview. It goes directly to the final Definition → Composition → completed Block → Program design. It does not ask you to reproduce any intermediate preview API.

If the application already uses an earlier Layers or Blocks preview, use [Upgrade an Earlier Preview](/preview-upgrade) instead.

The migration changes application assembly and effect wiring. Your Model remains the source of truth, Messages remain facts, update remains pure, and the Runtime still performs Commands after update returns them. The new structure makes those boundaries checkable across a complete child graph.

## Pin the Exact Preview

Use this integration preview's ready announcement and the banner at the top of the same deployed site to identify the target. The deployment's [`preview-release.json`](/preview-release.json) records the full source commit and the exact package map used to build the docs and embedded examples. # Workspace

A project workspace built from Foldkit Blocks. It includes issue lists and routed editors, a project board, comments, saved filters, members, notifications, project settings, and a command palette.

Run from the repository root after the normal install and package build:

```sh
pnpm dev:example:workspace
```

The example needs no credentials or database. An Effect Service starts with sixteen issues across three projects. Changes persist for the lifetime of that application Runtime and reset when the page reloads. Views use Tailwind through the same Vite integration as the other examples.

## Try the interactions

- Search, filter, sort, and group issues. The URL records those settings for copied links, reload, and browser history. Name the current view and choose **Save view** to add the preset to the sidebar.
- Open an issue, edit its title or properties, and save. Lists, My Issues, and project boards use the same canonical data. Issue rows, Board titles, and member assignments are native links, including open-in-new-tab and copy-link behavior. Closing returns to the complete filtered origin.
- Close an edited issue, visit another issue, or use browser Back. The sidebar keeps each issue's draft for the session, including an unsent comment. Reopen it to continue, or choose **Discard changes** or **Discard comment**.
- In Settings, choose **Fail next save** and wait for its acknowledgement. Then open and edit an issue. The draft survives the failed save; choose **Retry save** to finish saving.
- Choose **New issue** to open the Dialog. Creation updates shared data and opens the new issue.
- Open a project's board. Each column's plus button opens Create issue with that project and status selected. Drag an issue between status columns or reorder it. The card moves immediately while the save is pending. A failed save restores its position without replacing newer issue data. Use the drag handle with a pointer, or press Space to start keyboard dragging, arrow keys to reorder, Tab to switch columns, and Space to drop. Handles keep focus through saving.
- Add a comment while an issue draft is dirty. Comments and activity update the baseline without replacing editable fields. A conflicting change to those fields requires an explicit reload before resaving.
- Use Cmd/Ctrl+K to open the command palette, including while typing in another input. Search issues or projects, navigate results with arrow keys, and press Enter.
- Teammate activity arrives every 20 seconds after the workspace loads. Comments notify assignees and participants; assignments notify their recipient. Open **Notifications** to read an update and visit its issue, mark it unread again, or mark all of the active member’s notifications as read. Switching **Active member** changes whose inbox you see. Read notifications remain available. Settings can simulate the next event immediately.
- Open project settings, change its name or description, and save.
- Navigate between issues while a save is pending. Each issue keeps one editor Model for the session, so the hidden editor receives its result and settles before it is shown again. Results stay scoped to their issue ID and cannot update the editor currently on screen.

## Product design

The interface puts issues and the current task first. Page headers identify the view; descriptions explain actual project scope or a consequence. Controls need a complete workflow, including loading, failure, retry, and keyboard behavior. For example, a saved view restores grouping as well as its search and filters. Row selection is omitted until there is a useful bulk action.

On narrow screens, opening an issue shows its editor directly. Desktop layouts retain the list and editor together. Simulation controls live in Settings, and routine save feedback stays below the save actions.

Every single-selection control uses Foldkit UI Listbox: Active member, list filters, creation fields, and issue properties. They share rendering through `listbox.ts` and application-owned Tailwind component classes in `styles.css`. Command-palette results use the same option, focus, and disabled treatments. Compact controls vary their density deliberately. Foldkit UI supplies behavior without prescribing the application's visual style.

Status, priority, sort, grouping, and status-filter Listboxes specialize the existing `Listbox.create<Item, Value>()` factory. Their option Schemas and shared view helper preserve the domain value type through the Binding's `Selected` policy. Dynamic project, member, and encoded assignee values remain strings. Listbox's raw Message Schema still accepts strings, so the selection policies retain validation for malformed injected Messages; the generic argument alone cannot validate runtime input. Local filter Messages declare their domain Schemas directly and reject invalid values during decoding.

Creating an issue locks draft editing until the request settles. `editDraft` accepts a Model-to-Model callback, keeping ordinary `modifyFields` calls and their field validation at the call site. A rejected edit preserves the incoming Model object. `createIssue/draft.ts` supplies that policy to field updates and disabled controls. Submission separately prevents duplicate requests, and reopening a pending form preserves the submitted draft. Closing the Dialog remains available while creation is pending.

Issue and comment drafts survive internal navigation. Reloading or leaving the page requests the browser's native unsaved-work warning while drafts remain. Accepting that navigation discards the in-memory session; this is not durable storage, and browsers do not guarantee the warning in every exit situation.

See the [product review](../../internal/workspace-product-review.md) for the control decisions and remaining command-palette assessment. These are concrete consumer cases to assess before adding framework APIs.

## Ownership

The root Model owns the canonical workspace snapshot in `workspaceAsyncData`: issues, projects, and members. Loading, refreshing, and failed refreshes retain the appropriate data without a second cache. Lists, boards, the directory, and the palette receive that data as view inputs. Their Blocks own interaction state, such as Listbox focus, dragging, or the active command result. Applied issue filters belong to the Route and enter Issue List as view inputs.

The root uses AsyncData directly because its mutation handlers reconcile optimistic placement, rollback, live results, and issue revisions in that same snapshot. Query currently exposes fetch/reset operations without public retained-data reconciliation or settlement OutMessages for initializing routed children. The [Query assessment](../../internal/workspace-query-assessment.md) records that boundary.

The detail Block owns its editable draft, a baseline containing only editable fields and their revision, any conflicting field revision, and save feedback. The parent supplies the current Issue as view input, so comments keep updating while a field conflict preserves the draft. Its nested Comment Composer owns comment input and posting feedback. The root retains one keyed detail Model per visited issue and a lightweight draft projection reported through OutMessages for the sidebar and native exit warning. Keeping a draft does not create another authoritative issue collection. Successful mutations emit OutMessages; parent policy updates the canonical snapshot. Snapshot refreshes and multi-issue move responses reconcile every retained editor from the merged canonical data, including hidden editors, through Message-backed Binding operations. Conflicts are separate from failed save attempts.

# Block

## Overview

[](#overview)

A large application becomes difficult to change when every feature's transition logic accumulates in one update function. A Block keeps one feature's state machine together: its Model, Messages, update, Commands, view, and lifecycle work. Blocks preserve a single Application Model assembled from those owned child Models. The parent receives child Messages and decides how each feature participates in the larger application.

The child describes what it owns. The parent creates a Binding that describes the relationship between that child and the rest of the application.

Four values make those responsibilities visible:

| Value | Owner | What it decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | Feature | Model, Message, optional OutMessage and ChildInitContext contracts, Commands, lifecycle work, and Steps |
| Composition | Feature | The exact child Binding and Mount graph used by init, update, and the main view |
| Completed Block | Feature | The implementation and local handler recipe that a parent may bind |
| Binding | Parent | Model storage, child initializer arguments, delivery context, and OutMessage policy |

The Settings example on this page grows through that sequence. Settings first defines and completes its own state machine. Profile then creates `SettingsBinding`, registers it in `ApplicationComposition`, handles the `ChangedTheme` fact, and embeds the Settings view.

The sequence is Definition → Composition → preparation → assembly. A Definition establishes the contracts and authoring methods. A Composition fixes the child Binding and Mount graph. `prepareBlock` checks and packages the authored implementation as an opaque draft. `Block.assemble` finishes that draft as the branded Block accepted by Bindings, Programs, and Server rendering. The root follows the same sequence before `Program.make` or `Program.makeElement` adds host behavior.

Definitions, Compositions, Bindings, Blocks, and Programs are passive. `makeInit`, `makeUpdate`, and `makeView` return functions for the Runtime to call later. At the root, `program.provide(ApplicationLayer)` supplies ordinary Effect Services without building them. `Runtime.run`, `Runtime.hydrate`, or `Runtime.embed` builds the selected handler graph, resolves Flags when required, calls init, and begins performing effects.

A Binding lets Foldkit use one parent-owned policy across update, view, Subscriptions, ManagedResources, Mounts, and handler collection. The parent still decides where the child Model lives, what child facts mean, when the child exists, and where it renders.

If you are converting an existing suite alongside these production boundaries, the [testing migration cookbook](/testing#migrate-an-existing-test-suite) shows Command identity, generated child results, Subscription registries, and completed UI Block contracts before and after.

Its [client source](https://github.com/foldkit/foldkit/tree/main/packages/typing-game/client/src) shows Definitions split across files, parent Bindings, route gates, OutMessages, and root service provision.
